summary: Miqdaad bin Aswad refused to sit out jihaad because of his weight, citing the Qur'anic command to march out light or heavy, as Jubayr bin Nufayr reports.
notes: Text says Miqdaad bin Aswad; tagged as miqdaad-bin-amr, the approved entry for the same Companion. Please verify.

summary: Abdullaah bin Umar reports that Umar, overhearing a woman's lament at night, asked his daughter Hafsa how long a woman can be without her husband, then resolved not to keep an army away from home beyond that period.

Abdullaah bin Amr reports the du'aa the Prophet made as he set out for Badr with 315 men, asking Allaah to provide transport, clothing and food for his Companions, and how Allaah granted this after the victory.
Abu Sa'eed Khudri reports the du'aa the Prophet taught the Companions during the Battle of Khandaq, after which Allaah sent a powerful wind against the enemy.
Mu'aadh bin Jabal relates the Prophet's words on the reward of dhikr and spending in jihaad, and explains that spending while out on an expedition earns far more than spending from home.
notes: Abdur Rahmaan is one of the narrators in the chain and is not identified further in the text.

summary: Aasim bin Amr bin Qataadah tells how Quzmaan, whom the Prophet called a man of Jahannam, fought fiercely at Uhud only for his people's honour and then killed himself when his wound became unbearable.
Maalik bin Aws reports Umar's teaching that the reward of those who fall in an army depends on their intention, and that true martyrs are those who fight with perseverance seeking Allaah's reward.

Mu'aadh Juhani reports the Prophet's ruling that whoever crowds the camp or blocks a road earns no reward for jihaad, and a separate narration adds that the Companions stayed close together on campaign.
notes: The opening paragraph ('Another narration adds...') is a separate report with no named narrator, joined to Mu'aadh Juhani's report.

summary: Abu Sa'eed Khudri reports that Ubay bin Ka'b asked Allaah for a fever that would stay with him until death without preventing Hajj, Umrah, jihaad or congregational salaah, and it did.

Anas bin Maalik tells how his uncle Anas bin Nadhar, who missed Badr, fought at Uhud with over eighty wounds until he was martyred, and how a verse of the Qur'aan was understood to refer to men like him.
Qaasim bin Abdur Rahmaan reports that Anas bin Nadhar rebuked men who had lost heart after the report of the Prophet's martyrdom, then fought on until he was killed.

Jaabir reports that at Uhud, when only eleven Ansaar and Talha remained with the Prophet, Talha repeatedly volunteered to hold back the enemy, and the Prophet told him that saying Bismillaah would have lifted him to heaven.
Abdullaah bin Abbaas reports that after Uhud Ali brought his sword to Faatima, and the Prophet said that Sahal bin Hunayf and Abu Dujaana Simaak bin Harasha had also fought well.
Ubaydullaah bin Ka'b reports that at Khandaq Ali invited Amr bin Abd Wadd to Allaah, His Rasool and Islaam, and when Amr refused and taunted him, Ali fought and killed him in single combat.
Abdullaah bin Mas'ood says that at Badr Sa'd bin Abi Waqqaas fought alongside the Prophet both as cavalry and as infantry.
notes: The heading describes three men killed by one arrow at Uhud, but the text is about Badr and contains no arrow story.

summary: Jaabir Ru'ayni reports that Abu Bakr, seeing an army off, said that those who help prepare it, send it off and make du'aa for it share in the reward of going out in the path of Allaah.
notes: The heading names Usaama's army, but the text does not mention Usaama.

summary: Abdullaah bin Abbaas reports that the Prophet set out in Ramadhaan to conquer Makkah and kept fasting until he reached Kudayd.
Ummu Atiyya, who went on seven expeditions with the Prophet's army, describes how she cooked, nursed the wounded and tended the sick in the camp.
notes: The heading names Rubayyi bint Mu'awwidh and Layla Ghifaariyya, but the text contains only Ummu Atiyya.

summary: Anas reports that Ummu Sulaym kept a dagger with her at Hunayn to deal with any Mushrik who came near her, and that the Prophet smiled at her answer.
notes: The text says only 'Hadhrat Anas'; tagged as anas-bin-maalik, the usual Companion of that name. Please verify.

summary: Qataada reports that Uthmaan began praying four rakaahs at Mina, and that Abdullaah bin Mas'ood, though he recited Innaa lillaah, prayed four behind him, saying that causing division was worse.

Abdullaah bin Abbaas describes Umar's sigh and the qualities Umar named for a khalifah: strong without harshness, lenient without weakness, generous without extravagance, and careful with money without miserliness.
Abdullaah bin Abbaas recounts his questioning of Umar, who said that Ali had merits but that a khalifah must not compromise principles and must judge fairly even against his own people.
notes: Contains an abridgement cross-reference ('The narration then continues up to the point where...') followed by a separate saying of Umar.

summary: Salmaan testifies that Umar is a khalifah and not a king, and Ka'b, citing scripture, says the prophecy he found describes Umar as a khalifah in the pattern of prophethood before kingship.
notes: Salmaan's report and the account of a man from the Banu Asad are two reports of the same meeting, followed by Ka'b's statement. Ka'b is tagged as kab-ahbaar on the basis of his description as a scholar of earlier scriptures. Please verify.

summary: Sha'bi reports that Umar kept certain Quraysh confined to Madinah to protect the seat of khilaafah, that Uthmaan released them and they scattered, and the text then records Umar's and others' counsel to the Prophet on the caravan of Abu Sufyaan and on the Badr prisoners, including the revelation on ransom.
notes: Many separate reports are joined (Sha'bi, Qais bin Abi Haazim, Anas, Ibn Mas'ood and others). The text is also cut off mid-verse at the end ('Surah Anfaal, verses').

summary: Abu Hurayrah reports that when Haarith of the Banu Ghitfaan demanded half the produce of Madinah, the Prophet consulted four leading Sa'ds, and Haarith's party answered with an accusation of betrayal.
notes: A separate closing line from Musaddad reports something from Umar about nights spent with Abu Bakr.

summary: Abu Khuzayma bin Thaabit reports that Umar set conditions for his governors on appointment, forbidding Turkish horses, fine flour, fine clothing and locked doors to the needy, and reminded them they were sent to establish salaah, share the spoils and judge justly.
notes: Begins 'Hadhrat (RA) states' with the narrator's name missing, and includes a separate similar narration in which Abu Khuzayma bin Thaabit reports the appointment ceremony.

summary: Abu Salama reports Umar's oath that he would have executed anyone who killed a Mushrik after pointing to him as a sign of safety and then surrendering to him.
notes: The heading is garbled OCR. The word 'sty' in the text is probably OCR debris for a gesture word and was not relied on. Abu Salama is tagged as abu-salma-bin-abdir-rahmaan, not as a Companion. Please verify.

summary: Anas bin Maalik says that Hurmuzaan, who surrendered at Tustar, was spared by Umar after Anas gave testimony that Hurmuzaan had been promised amnesty, and Hurmuzaan then accepted Islaam and received an allowance.
Abul Furaat reports that Uthmaan asked his slave to twist his ear in retribution, and when the slave did so gently Uthmaan told him to twist harder, praising the delight of retribution in this world.
notes: Text stops mid-sentence ('...without any in the').

summary: The text traces Abu Bakr's life as khalifah: he gave up trade for a fixed allowance, returned public money on his deathbed, and on his Umrah visit to Makkah was greeted by its leaders while his father Abu Quhaafa wept with joy.
notes: A biography compiled from several episodes and sources (life as khalifah, deathbed, Umrah and Hajj in 12 AH).

summary: On the Prophet's advice, Abu Talha divided his beloved orchard at Bir Haa among his relatives and nephews.
notes: Opens with 'Another narration of Bukhari adds', so the narration it adds to is not in this text.

summary: Abu Hurayrah reports that a hungry Ansaari guest was hosted by an Ansaari man and his wife, who put out their lamp and pretended to eat so the guest could eat, and Allaah praised their conduct and revealed the verse about preferring others.

Uthmaan reports that the blind Haaritha bin Numaan gave charity to beggars with his own hand, guided by a string, because the Prophet had said that giving to the poor personally saves one from a gruesome death.

Urwa reports that Sa'd bin Ubaadah would announce from his house an open invitation to anyone wanting meat or fat, that his son did the same after him, and that Abdullaah bin Umar confirmed no one was as generous as that father and son.
notes: Urwa is not identified further. The text does not give enough to choose between the Urwa entries in the approved list.

summary: Jahjaa Ghifaari, who came to accept Islaam, recounts how the Prophet hosted him and his group, and the Prophet explained that a believer eats to fill one intestine while a disbeliever eats to fill seven.
Anas reports that when dates were brought to the Prophet, he shared them with the Companions while eating quickly, apparently because he was about to leave.
notes: The text says only 'Hadhrat Anas'; tagged as anas-bin-maalik, the usual Companion of that name. Please verify.

summary: Jaabir reports that Qais bin Sa'd bin Ubaadah slaughtered seven camels to feed his hungry expedition, and that on the shore they then found a giant fish which fed them for three days.
Ja'far bin Burqaan reports that Abdur Rahmaan bin Auf freed thirty families of slaves, after an opening saying of the Prophet about who will show compassion to his people after his death.
notes: Opens with a separate saying of the Prophet, then Ja'far bin Burqaan's report. The Banu Zuhrah incident named in the heading is not in the text.

summary: Ibraheem bin Abdur Rahmaan bin Auf reports that when the treasures of Kisra were brought to Umar, Umar wept, saying that Allaah sets enmity between a nation when it is given such wealth, while Abdur Rahmaan bin Auf tried to comfort him.
Abdullaah bin Umar reports that when Umar was given a gold-laden table cloth to distribute, he wept, fearing it was a test rather than a blessing.
